title: A Designer Rebuilt Her Family’s Vermont Ski Chalet After a Fire

content: Photo by Read McKendree This article is from the winter 2027 issue of Boston Home . Sign up here to receive a subscription. Interior designer Kaitlin Smith never expected to design her family’s Vermont ski house twice. She and her husband had bought the 1970s chalet in Plymouth during the pandemic, drawn to its timber-frame character and majestic setting on a former ski mountain, where an old trail runs practically through their backyard. “The home is very private; you look out the windows, and all you see are mountains, and in the summer, there are beautiful wildflowers and ferns—it’s the views that really got us,” says Smith, who, along with her husband, is a lifelong skier. After spending a few years in the home, they had just begun making updates when a fire destroyed the house. No one was hurt, but the weekend retreat where they envisioned spending their children’s ski years was suddenly gone. Starting over presented Smith with a choice: reinvent the house or bring back what her family had loved about it. She chose the latter. “We just wanted to rebuild the original house as close as possible,” she says, noting that she was slightly daunted about finding a builder who could get started right away. “There was a lot of building going on in Vermont—everyone seemed to have bought during COVID.” Fortunately, builder Carl Lavallee returned her call. “He said, ‘Am I reading this note on my desk correctly? Your house burned down?’” He was struck by the family’s story and signed on to the project immediately. The plan called for re-creating the chalet’s gabled roof, deep overhangs, oversize windows, and distinctive balusters while improving the few things that hadn’t worked before. The 1900s oak trestle dining table is paired with antique spindle-back chairs. The antler-inspired chandelier was a score from the Brimfield Antique Show. The mudroom cabinetry features a cutout detail that nods to the Swiss styling of the original house. The wall and back door are painted in Benjamin Moore’s “Norway Spruce.” Impervious soapstone was selected for the counter material, while cabinets are painted in Benjamin Moore’s “Wedgewood Gray.” In place of a typical kitchen island, Smith opted for a slim oak table topped with butcher-block to offer additional prep space. The just-under-2,000-square-foot house retains its “upside-down” plan, with the kitchen, dining, and living areas on the second floor where vaulted ceilings and expansive windows take advantage of mountain views. The interior is almost entirely clad in wood—Douglas fir beams, oak floors, and pine-paneled walls—while an oversize fieldstone fireplace anchors the living room. Smith wanted the newly rebuilt house to feel as though it had “been on the mountain forever, full of collected treasures and plenty of stories and memories.” Those treasures are everywhere. Nearly all the furniture is antique or vintage, much of it found at Vermont antiques shops and flea markets. An early-1900s oak trestle table came from Stone House Antique Center in nearby Chester; an oversize antler chandelier above it was a Brimfield Antique Show discovery. American folk art, old quilts, baskets, painted furniture, and Smith’s collection of ceramic and brass animals add to the sense that the rooms evolved over decades rather than months. In the main living room, a comfy custom sectional, upholstered in Kravet fabric, slides just under the windows. Lamps with Pooky x GP & J Baker shades provide another burst of color. In Smith’s son’s room, walls are sheathed in a jubilant plaid Thibaut wallcovering. The bed belonged to Smith’s husband when he was a child. Another antler-inspired chandelier is from Woodland Creek. For Smith, who owns a design shop in Watch Hill and whose work often skews coastal, the mountain house also offered a chance to experiment. “Doing our ski house was totally switching gears for me,” she says. Against the abundance of warm wood, she layered saturated reds, blues, and greens with florals, ginghams, plaids, and traditional Nordic-inspired prints. “I could play with bold colors that I wouldn’t always put together here,” she says. A guest room, for instance, mixes blue plaid with red and blue florals and an heirloom quilt handmade by Smith’s great-grandmother, in which no two pieces are alike. Other family pieces carry their own histories. A handpainted walnut bed, dubbed the “Bunny Bed,” belonged to Smith’s husband as a child and now sits in her son’s room against green plaid wallpaper. A copper sink her mother hauled home from Paris’s Clignancourt flea market finally found its place here, too. “It may leak a bit,” Smith admits, “but we still love it!” In the bunk room, dual double beds are situated under twin beds up top. The beds and the wall behind them are painted in Benjamin Moore’s “Jamestown Blue”; coverlets from Ida Mae Home are paired with bed skirts in a red Sister Parish motif. With three children and a dog, however, nostalgia couldn’t trump practicality. Wool fabrics stand up to ski-house life, gathered bed skirts conceal storage, and Smith designed a bunk room with twin beds above full-size beds to accommodate extra guests. Downstairs, a den anchored by the family’s well-loved leather sectional gives the kids a place of their own after skiing. Upstairs, everyone gravitates back to the fireplace. Surrounded by plush seating, vivid patterns, vintage finds, and those mountain views, it is exactly the kind of room Smith set out to create: one where nothing feels too precious to actually live in.
